question: In one or two sentences: how does the default position of an Azure network security group differ from the default position of an AWS security group, and why must an administrator know which applies?

question: Under a default-deny (allow-list) firewall policy, which of the following holds?

question: Name two capabilities of a next-generation firewall (NGFW) that a plain stateful firewall such as ufw or a cloud security group does not have.

question: Which option best describes the Zero Trust strategy?

option_b: Nobody and nothing is trusted merely for its position on the network; every user, device, application and transaction is checked again and again, assuming breach

question: Building on the chapter exercise "SSH brute force as threat-risk-control": your team's VM runs Nginx on port 80 and SSH on port 22, and a colleague has additionally opened the database port 5432 "temporarily, for testing" and left it open. The VM sits in an Azure virtual network alongside other team resources. Using the chapter's three common firewall mistakes and the discussion of provider defaults, identify every way this machine is more exposed than it should be, and give the full ufw command sequence (including the rule from the exercise) that establishes the intended default-deny policy.
sample_answer: Exposures: (i) the forgotten database port 5432 (second common mistake); (ii) SSH open to the whole Internet instead of only the administrator's address (first mistake, the brute-force risk); (iii) the Azure default (third mistake): NSG built-in rules allow east-west traffic within the virtual network, so other VNet resources may reach the VM even without added rules. Sequence: sudo ufw default deny incoming; sudo ufw default allow outgoing; sudo ufw allow from YOUR_IP to any port 22 proto tcp; sudo ufw allow 80/tcp; sudo ufw enable; then sudo ufw status to read the loaded policy back. Full credit needs all three exposures, the restricted SSH rule, no rule for 5432, and the read-back.
